FIRST WARN FORECAST
Monday, August 24, 2026

First. Accurate. Trusted.

A NICE START TO THE WEEK

We are beginning the final full week of August with another pretty nice late-summer day across Missouri and Illinois. Temperatures will be seasonably warm, humidity remains manageable, and most of us will stay dry.

High pressure that brought us the comfortable weekend is slowly shifting east toward the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley. As it moves away, our winds will gradually turn toward the east and southeast. That will eventually begin the process of bringing warmer air and a little more moisture back into the region.

For Monday, though, there really is not much to complain about.

High temperatures will generally reach the lower to middle 80s across central Missouri, the St. Louis metro, southeast Missouri, and southern Illinois. Skies will range from partly to mostly sunny.

There are a few isolated showers across western Missouri early this morning, but they should have difficulty making much progress eastward. For the vast majority of the First Warn Weather coverage area, Monday will be dry.

Tonight will be a little warmer than the past couple of nights as our wind begins turning toward the southeast. Lows will generally fall into the lower to middle 60s.

A LITTLE WARMER TUESDAY

Temperatures begin creeping upward Tuesday as the large-scale weather pattern slowly shifts.

We should see afternoon temperatures climb into the middle 80s across much of the region, with a few warmer locations potentially reaching the upper 80s.

Most of Tuesday should remain dry. Our attention then turns to Tuesday night as a disturbance approaches from the northwest.

There is a 20 to 30 percent chance for showers and thunderstorms Tuesday night into Wednesday. The ingredients for thunderstorms Tuesday night are not particularly impressive, so widespread activity is far from guaranteed.

That changes somewhat Wednesday.

WATCHING WEDNESDAY FOR THUNDERSTORMS

A weak cold front will begin moving south through the Mississippi Valley Wednesday as an upper-level disturbance moves across the Midwest and into the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley.

Temperatures ahead of the front should climb into the middle and upper 80s. Instability will also increase considerably, with some guidance suggesting CAPE values exceeding 2,000 J/kg.

There is one big question: Can thunderstorms actually develop?

A layer of warm air aloft may act as a cap over the atmosphere. Think of it as a lid on a boiling pot. We can have plenty of heat and moisture underneath, but as long as that lid stays firmly in place, thunderstorms have difficulty developing.

Right now, the forcing associated with Wednesday's front does not look particularly strong. That is why rain chances remain relatively low at around 20 to 30 percent.

However, if that cap breaks, the atmosphere will have enough instability to support more widespread thunderstorm development than those rain chances might suggest.

Wind shear should be around 30 knots, which would also be sufficient for some organization. Because of that, any thunderstorms that manage to develop Wednesday could become strong to severe.

It is not a situation that warrants sounding the alarms at this point, but Wednesday is certainly a day we will be watching.

Damaging winds would likely be the primary concern if stronger storms develop.

SLIGHTLY COOLER AND DRIER BEHIND THE FRONT

The cold front should move through the region Wednesday into Thursday, but do not expect a dramatic temperature drop behind it.

Thursday and Friday will probably only be about 2 to 3 degrees cooler than Wednesday. High temperatures should remain comfortably in the 80s.

The more noticeable change will be the humidity.

Drier air will move into Missouri and Illinois behind the front, allowing overnight temperatures to fall back into the upper 50s and lower 60s in many locations by Friday morning.

So while the afternoons will remain warm, mornings should feel pretty comfortable toward the end of the work week.

SUMMER MAY TURN UP THE HEAT THIS WEEKEND

There are some interesting signals showing up for next weekend.

As the large ridge over the western United States begins expanding east, temperatures should start climbing again Saturday and Sunday.

Some of our guidance is becoming fairly aggressive with the heat, suggesting upper 80s and lower 90s Saturday followed by widespread lower to middle 90s Sunday.

Even some of the cooler ensemble solutions are suggesting temperatures in the lower to middle 90s Sunday afternoon.

That certainly gets my attention.

There is still a fairly large spread among the models, so confidence in exactly how hot we become next weekend is not particularly high yet. We are several days away, and small changes in the upper-level pattern could make a noticeable difference in our temperatures.

For now, I would plan on a warming trend this weekend and keep an eye on Sunday in particular.

August may have one more reminder for us that September has not arrived just yet.

THE BOTTOM LINE

Monday will be another pleasant late-summer day with partly to mostly sunny skies and highs in the lower to middle 80s across central Missouri, the St. Louis metro, southeast Missouri, and southern Illinois.

Temperatures gradually warm Tuesday and Wednesday, with highs reaching the middle and upper 80s by Wednesday.

Our next opportunity for thunderstorms arrives Tuesday night into Wednesday as a weak cold front approaches. Rain chances are only around 20 to 30 percent because a cap may prevent widespread thunderstorm development.

However, if thunderstorms can break through that cap Wednesday, there will be enough instability and wind shear for some storms to become strong or severe. We will watch that possibility closely as we get closer.

Slightly cooler and noticeably drier air arrives Thursday and Friday before temperatures begin climbing again next weekend.

And yes, some of the guidance is trying to bring the 90s back by Saturday and Sunday.

Summer apparently noticed how much we enjoyed this past weekend and took it personally.

First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Threat Levels

Southern Illinois

Missouri Bootheel
Far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border
Areas south of Poplar Bluff and near Paducah
Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.
